abstract: Brain tumor growth induces considerable deformation of the surrounding tissue, yet the mechanical contribution of intracranial dural structures and the influence of tumor material heterogeneity on mass effect remain poorly understood. In this study, we developed a heterogeneous finite element model of the brain to investigate the mechanical role of the falx cerebri and tentorium cerebelli and to determine how variations in tumor subregion stiffness influence the mechanical response of the brain. Two complementary analyses were performed. First, synthetic lesion models with and without the falx and tentorium were compared under otherwise identical conditions. Inclusion of these structures produced only minor changes in global displacement magnitude, but substantially altered the spatial distribution of stress. The dural structures acted as stiff internal partitions that limited interhemispheric and supratentorial-infratentorial deformation and modified load transmission throughout the brain. Including the dural structures led to a different pattern of ventricular volume change during tumor growth, with both lateral ventricles compressed in the dura-included model, whereas without the dura the ventricle on the tumor side expanded while the opposite ventricle was compressed. Second, a parametric analysis was performed using MRI-informed patient-specific tumors comprising necrotic tumor core (NTC), contrast-enhancing tumor core (ETC), and peritumoral edema (Ed). Variations in ETC stiffness produced the largest and most spatially distributed changes in displacement and von Mises stress, with stronger effects in ETC-dominant tumors. Edema stiffness produced weaker and more diffuse effects, whereas NTC stiffness mainly affected the principal stretch within the tumor. These findings demonstrate that intracranial dural structures alter the distribution of tumor-induced deformation and stress despite their limited influence on global displacement magnitude. In the patient-specific models, varying the tumor stiffness within its reported range changed the mechanical response by only a few percent, with the ETC having the largest influence.
